title: Outcomes of a hypertension care program based on task-sharing with private pharmacies: a retrospective study from two blocks in rural India
abstract: Low density of formal care providers in rural India results in restricted and delayed access to standardized management of hypertension. Task-sharing with pharmacies, typically the first point of contact for rural populations, can bridge the gap in access to formal care and improve health outcomes. In this study, we implemented a hypertension care program involving task-sharing with twenty private pharmacies between November 2020 and April 2021 in two blocks of Bihar, India. Pharmacists conducted free hypertension screening, and a trained physician offered free consultations at the pharmacy. We calculated the number of subjects screened, initiated on treatment (enrolled) and the change in blood pressure using the data collected through the program application. Of the 3403 subjects screened at pharmacies, 1415 either reported having a history of hypertension or had elevated blood pressure during screening. Of these, 371 (26.22%) were enrolled in the program. Of these, 129 (34.8%) made at least one follow-up visit. For these subjects, the adjusted average difference in systolic and diastolic blood pressure between the screening and follow-up visits was -11.53 (-16.95 to -6.11, 95% CI) and -4.68 (-8.53 to -0.82, 95% CI) mmHg, respectively. The adjusted odds of blood pressure being under control in this group during follow-up visits compared to screening visit was 7.07 (1.29 to 12.85, 95% CI). Task-sharing with private pharmacies can lead to early detection and improved control of blood pressure in a resource-constrained setting. Additional strategies to increase patient screening and retention rates are needed to ensure sustained health benefits.

summary.oneLiner: Task-sharing with 20 private pharmacies in rural Bihar was associated with lower blood pressure among enrolled patients who returned for follow-up, though retention was low.
summary.overview: The study looked at a hypertension program in which pharmacists in 20 private pharmacies in two rural Bihar blocks screened people for free and a physician visited monthly to diagnose and prescribe. Of 3,403 people screened, 1,415 were potentially hypertensive and 371 enrolled, but only 129 (about 35% of enrolled) returned for at least one follow-up. Among those 129, blood pressure fell on average and the odds of being under control were higher at follow-up than at screening. The authors describe this as a retrospective cohort study without a comparison group, so the changes cannot be attributed to the program alone. Patient retention was the main weakness they identified.
summary.question: Can task-sharing with private pharmacies, where pharmacists screen and a physician consults, help detect hypertension early and improve blood pressure control in rural India?
summary.method: A retrospective cohort study using programme data from a pharmacy-based hypertension care program. The authors reported operational outcomes (screening, consultation, enrolment, follow-up) descriptively and estimated changes in systolic and diastolic blood pressure and the odds of controlled blood pressure using linear and logistic regressions, both unadjusted and adjusted for patient fixed effects, with standard errors clustered by pharmacy.
summary.data: Programme records from 20 private pharmacies in Behea and Udwantnagar blocks of Bhojpur district, Bihar, India, collected between 23 November 2020 and 30 April 2021. Of 3,403 screened subjects, 1,415 were potentially hypertensive, 371 enrolled, and 129 with at least one follow-up visit formed the clinical analysis sample.
findings: Of 3,403 people screened, 1,415 were potentially hypertensive and 371 (26.22%) enrolled in the program.
Of the enrolled, 129 (34.8%) made at least one follow-up visit.
Adjusted average change in systolic blood pressure between screening and follow-up was -11.53 mmHg (95% CI -16.95 to -6.11); diastolic was -4.68 mmHg (95% CI -8.53 to -0.82).
Adjusted odds of blood pressure being under control at follow-up versus screening were 7.07 (95% CI 1.29 to 12.85).

The authors state that task-sharing with private pharmacies 'can lead to early detection and improved control of blood pressure', and that additional strategies to increase screening and retention are needed.
The authors note the study lacked a comparator group and that the COVID-19 second wave may have reduced screenings and retention.
summary.whyItMatters: The authors suggest the model offers policymakers a plausible way to work with the private sector to expand hypertension care in areas with weak public health delivery, and argue for public investment in such task-sharing programs. They emphasise that improving patient retention and aligning pharmacist and patient incentives are needed for success, and note that the program did not pay pharmacies or cover patients' medication costs.
